@@128676272 <p> Was Miles Davis 's In A Silent Way the first known example of what we now call ambient jazz ? It has all the hallmarks : electro-acoustic improvisation that sets a sustained mood , running over an extended period without being overly hung up on rhythmic or harmonic changes , and which can serve as soothing background ambience while also meriting closer listening if the urge strikes . <p> You could also make a case for some of Don Cherry 's work with Collin Walcott and Nana Vasconcelos in the trio Codona , whose albums for the ECM label created pristine soundscapes using a variety of non-western instruments . And there 's Paul Horn , whose groundbreaking 1976 solo flute recording , Inside The Great Pyramid , established him as a leading figure in the nascent New Age movement . <p> In recent years , a new crop of musicians has been marketed as ambient jazz , who also lean heavily into the New Age vibe , incorporating soft-focus synth sheen into meditative vistas while maintaining elements of jazz-adjacent jams . Unsurprisingly , the New Age-friendly West Coast of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Los Angeles serving as the epicentre of this quiet earthquake . <p> Chief among LA 's practitioners has been percussionist/producer Carlos Ni ? o . Though active in music for decades , he 's gained visibility with recent albums like More Energy Fields , Current ( 2021 ) and Extra Presence ( 2022 ) , both credited to Carlos Ni ? o &amp; Friends -- a catch-all name for his ever-revolving cast of close collaborators from the fertile LA scene . More recently , he 's played on and co-produced the most controversial addition to the ambient jazz canon , Andr ? 3000 's opinion-splitting 2023 solo flute joint , New Blue Sun and , just this year , he released Openness Trio -- alongside guitarist Nate Mercereau and saxophonist Josh Johnson -- on the Blue Note label . <p> This new live date brings the idea out of the studio and into an outdoor setting where musicianship is nakedly paramount . It was recorded in LA 's Coldwater Canyon Park on the grounds of longstanding conservationist organisation TreePeople and features a seven-piece group of LA-based musical Friends , including @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the music they make does little to dispel the notion of ambient jazz sounding like the soundtrack to a bougie yoga retreat . Shakers and gongs . Chimes and cymbals . Hand drums quietly clopping . Breathy flutes and sinuous twin sax lines chasing their own tails . Ethereal tuned percussion . Wafting electronic tones . You get the idea . <p> But it does n't matter , because this session is entirely dominated by the voice of poet , writer , actor , filmmaker , rapper and all-round Renaissance Man , Saul Williams . As Williams ' spoken recitation unfolds , the improvised background subtly -- almost subliminally -- mirrors his words but never intrudes or distracts . Gentle rhythmic figures occasionally arise , with tuned percussion suggesting minimalist cycles . Rarer still , the saxes rise up in a brief crescendo . But , for the most part , it 's a hypnotically continuous bed of sound that gives Williams centre stage -- a position he occupies with grace and authority . <p> Slowly and deliberately , he repeats the opening incantation of " Land back " three @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ instantly setting an anti-colonial agenda . From there , he begins to paint an unsettling portrait of 21st-century evil . As befits the setting , he sketches a ghoulishly complacent , climate-denying administration , staffed by " President of archaeological indifference / ... Minister of the deteriorating sky / ... Bishop of the great Climate War . " <p> A sudden switch conflates colonial atrocities in Gaza and the US : " The voices beneath the rubble / the bones beneath this stage . " Then we 're confronted with the incomprehensible horror of genocide : " I had not imagined the bloodshed / I had not imagined the screams / the recorded sounds of children 's voices ... I could never imagine such deviance . " Faced with such entwined atrocities , despair is inevitable : " Look what they did to the land / what they did to the people / it was an impossible time / there was no way out of it / no way around . " What to do in a world so horribly out of joint ? " How to harmonise the planet @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ trauma , of not letting it consume you : " Air it out / Let it breathe . " And , gently , Williams begins to emerge as an avatar of coming change , with a liberatory incantation : " I speak a new language / as is always the first sign / of a new age . " Now we 're moving into Burroughsian strategies for taking back control : " Hack into the rebellious gene / ... Hack into doctrine / ... Hack into God . " Pretty soon , we have a psychic guerilla movement : " ... fully aware / of the world that we are stepping into / the times that we are walking into / unafraid . " <p> Williams delivers a concise lecture on how the Dutch East India Trade Company -- " the first multinational corporation " -- swindled the Lenape people out of the island of Manhattan , building a wall to keep them out on the site that is now Wall Street , where once slaves were rented daily . It climaxes in a desperate manifesto of letting go and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ find ourselves / ... rooting for the end of empire / I 've seen enough " -- with the saxophones reaching for a stark crescendo . <p> The poet Aja Monet briefly takes the mic , taking aim at " the hush money / howl of advertisements / electoral politics of greed / godless truths , " and assuring us that " the water is rising / ... money perishes in the face of the flood . " Then Williams returns with a crystalline parable about a firing squad with one member who " holds his fire / his dilemma / was my system of belief " -- offering us a glimpse of resistance , an example of doing the right thing . <p> These are stirring and urgent dramas , powerfully delivered . Though both Williams and Monet identify as poets , it 's scarcely relevant how their words might appear on a page . With an emphasis on raw performance , these bars owe more to the spoken word scene and slam poetry -- something Williams helped to popularise with the 1998 film , SLAM , which he @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ than that . Williams is pushing back past hip hop , past the Black Arts Movement , past Langston Hughes and the Harlem Renaissance , to the root of African American oral traditions . Back to the use of speech as a way of maintaining identity and resisting oppression . Of finding ways to survive . Together . <p> It all comes together in Williams ' last , exhortatory address to the audience , after the performance has ended : " I see no reason really for us to ... wallow in any sort of fear in terms of what lies ahead . I think we have to actually bask in community ... we have to make a change ... Prepare yourself for the transformative work and the transformative healing that this nation needs . " <p> Right now , these are the kinds of optimistic , pragmatic and inspiring words that everyone -- and not just America -- needs to hear .

@@128709616 <p> Kenneth Roth has never been shy . As an undergraduate at Brown University and later at Yale Law School , he was known for his sharp intellect , courage , and relentless curiosity . <p> His early legal career - four years in the US Attorney 's Office for the Southern District of New York , one of the country 's most prominent federal prosecutor 's offices - laid the foundation for a life dedicated to justice and , ultimately , to reshaping the global human rights movement . <p> For 30 years as the head of Human Rights Watch ( HRW ) , Roth became one of the world 's most formidable advocates for the voiceless . <p> Unlike many of his peers in government or at the United Nations , Roth feared no one . <p> He would walk into the offices of secretary-generals , prime ministers , and presidents and hold them to account on their obligations under international law . <h> New MEE newsletter : Jerusalem Dispatch <h> Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine , alongside Turkey Unpacked and other @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ UN High Commissioner for Human Rights " timid " , a bluntness that reflected his refusal to tolerate inaction in the face of abuse . <p> Roth did n't just " name and shame " abusive regimes ; he also challenged colleagues who hesitated to confront power . <p> Always measured - never shrill - he rooted his arguments in the law , lending weight and clarity to his words and making him one of the most influential voices on global human rights . <p> He rightly earned the nickname " the Godfather of Human Rights " . <p> When Roth stepped down from HRW after building it into an organisation with the influence and reach of a small state , he did not pause . <p> Instead , he wrote Righting Wrongs , a sweeping debut memoir that is , in many ways , his magnum opus . <p> The book chronicles the strategies and battles that defined his tenure , but it is also a meditation on persistence and how to keep fighting for justice in an era of impunity . <p> Roth never appears to grow depressed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of a long-distance runner . <p> Roth takes readers through some of the most pivotal moments of modern history : The post-Kuwait invasion period under Saddam Hussein ; @@128709938 <p> CHRIS SEARLE encourages you to go hear a landmark performance , and introduces some of the musicians <p> THE power of the war photograph is that it wo n't let you look away . And nowhere is this proving truer than in Gaza . <p> Photographs coming out of Gaza since October 2023 have communicated the severity of the destruction : collapsed buildings , bodies in shrouds , dead and maimed children and bombed-out hospitals and shelters . There have also been viral AI-generated images , such as All Eyes on Rafah . <p> But none of these galvanised the public as much as the photographic evidence of Israel 's systemic starvation of Gazans . Between April and July , more than 20,000 people in Gaza were hospitalised for malnutrition , including 3,000 children in life-threatening conditions . These photographs are a visual condensation of collective suffering that is impossible to ignore or deny . This is what makes them so powerful . <p> War photography is often impactful because it communicates the brutalities of war with visual mastery . Photographic elements such as composition , timing , tone @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that is full of intent . <p> This is what US photographer and curator John Szarkowski called " the photographer 's eye , " and what French photographer Henri Cartier Bresson coined as " the decisive moment . " It is to know where to point the camera , when to release the shutter and how to select the " right " image to release into the world . <p> Image <p> BARBARIC : Abdou Hussain Saad Faleh is tortured by Staff Sergeants Frederick and Harmann who took the picture " for fun " . The hooded detainee was told that he would be electrocuted if he fell off the box . Pic : US Government/CC <p> An iconic war photograph often reproduces a pose or gesture that is familiar to the popular imagination -- particularly through iconic religious imagery . Think of the horrifying photos that came out of Abu Ghraib prison during the Iraq war , where one tortured prisoner was photographed in the pose of Christ on the cross . <p> This was equally true of the 1972 image of Phan Thi Kim Phuc , the naked @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Such photographs can change the course of war . They often shape how wars are remembered , even when there is controversy around their truthfulness and authorship , as we have seen with the contested image of Kim Phuc . <p> The " napalm girl " photo shows terrified children , including nine-year-old Kim Phuc , as they run down a road after an aerial napalm attack by the South Vietnamese air force on June 8 1972 . <p> Historically , there have been many controversies over the staging of war photographs . Robert Capa 's Falling Soldier ( Loyalist Militiaman at the Moment of Death , Cerro Muriano , September 5 1936 ) is one of the most famous and yet disputed images in the history of war photography . <p> It purports to show a soldier shot dead mid-fall during the Spanish civil war . But historians suggest the man might have been posing , not dying . Whether it is real or staged remains unresolved . Still , it circulates as though it is true -- reminding us that the myths of war are just as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is remembered . <p> Photos are limited by their inability to convey sound , smell or any broader context . A staged photo might , at times , be even more effective than an unstaged one in conveying the lived experience of a war -- even if the ethics of the staging are dubious . <p> Photos and video from Gaza continue to circulate on social media , despite Israel barring foreign journalists from entering Gaza . <p> Israeli authorities have killed Palestinian journalists in record numbers . Yet this visual censorship has not stopped citizen journalists and organisations such as Activestills from sharing the atrocities in Gaza . <p> In Gaza , control over imagery has become part of the conflict . Al Jazeera was banned from operating inside Israel . Social media platform Meta has been found silencing posts from Palestinian accounts , with graphic images increasingly being labelled with warnings such as " sensitive content . " <p> So , what does it mean to be advised to look away from something someone else is living ? <p> As we know from the World War II , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ camp survivors during the Holocaust were used to prosecute Nazis at the Nuremberg trials . <p> But the meaning of war photographs also depends on timing , context , who controls what is shown and where the photos are distributed . <p> US gender studies scholar Judith Butler argues Western media weaponise images to construct a hierarchy of grief that determines whose life is publicly mourned . <p> Publishing a war photograph is not just an act of documentation -- it 's an act of interpretation . It shapes what others think is happening . In their book Picturing Atrocity ( Reaktion Books , 2011 ) , Nancy Miller and colleagues ask us how we can witness suffering without turning it into spectacle . <p> The book raises important ethical questions . Who owns an image of someone suffering ? What if the person photographed has died ? What if the image perpetuates violence that hurts those closest to it ? <p> A war photograph does not stop a missile . It does not feed a starving child . But it can interrupt denial and silence . <p> It can @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " you can not say you did n't know . " <p> Sara Oscar is a senior lecturer in visual communication at the School of Design , University of Technology Sydney ; Cherine Fahd is associate professor of visual communication at the University of Technology Sydney . <p> This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons licence .

@@128715856 <p> Israel 's war with Hamas began on October 7 , 2023 , after Hamas surprised the IDF , infiltrated Israel , murdered and kidnapped civilians in their homes and at a music festival , raped women , and burned children alive . Before any discussion of the future , it is worth remembering how this war began . <p> In response to this invasion , Israel declared war , with the stated goals to destroy Hamas as a military organisation , return the hostages ( over 250 at the start of the war ) , and prevent Hamas from continuing its rule over Gaza . The fighting dragged on longer than initially expected , but during this conflict Israel also dealt severe blows to Hezbollah in Lebanon , leaving the group now under pressure from the Lebanese government to disarm . It now operates as a guerrilla organisation . @@128721963 <h> UK Government has lost the plot if it 's criminalising this T-shirt <p> Screenwriter Paul Laverty pictured wearing a ' Genocide in Palestine , time to take action ' T-shirt in Edinburgh Image : Supplied <p> This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today , and has been written by our American colleagues . It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald . <p> THE arrest of Scottish screenwriter Paul Laverty for wearing a T-shirt reading " Genocide in Palestine -- time to take action " at a peaceful gathering should alarm anyone who cares about the rule of law in Scotland . Political speech -- especially speech about war , human rights and the conduct of states -- sits at the core of Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights ( ECHR ) . It merits the highest protection because democracy needs dissent . As the European Court of Human Rights put it in Handyside v United Kingdom ( 1976 ) , freedom of expression applies not only to information and ideas that are favourably @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that " offend , shock or disturb " . That principle is the price of pluralism , tolerance and broad-mindedness . <p> Two points deserve emphasis . First , the UK Government 's recent proscription of " Palestine Action " under the Terrorism Act 2000 can not lawfully be used as a dragnet to criminalise generic , non-violent expressions of conscience . Proscription is a blunt power ; its use must be tightly policed against overreach , as UN experts and domestic commentators have warned . <p> Second , even within the terrorism framework , the Crown must prove very specific statutory elements . Section 12(1) criminalises " inviting support " for a proscribed organisation . Parliament later added section 12(1A) ( in 2019 ) to reach the expression of an opinion or belief supportive of a proscribed group where the speaker is reckless as to whether the audience will be encouraged to support it . Section 13 is different again : it concerns clothing or articles displayed in such a way as to arouse reasonable suspicion that a person is a member or supporter of a proscribed organisation . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Here those elements matter . The slogan on Mr Laverty 's shirt did not refer to " Palestine Action " at all . It was a moral exhortation to act to stop what many -- including the International Court of Justice -- have described as a plausible risk of genocide in Gaza . Liability under section 12(1A) requires more than a generalised call to " take action " : it requires expression that is supportive of the proscribed organisation itself and , critically , recklessness as to whether the audience will be encouraged to support that organisation . Likewise , Section 13 requires clothing or an article to be worn or displayed in circumstances arousing reasonable suspicion of membership or support for the proscribed body ; a generic anti-genocide slogan does not meet that threshold . <p> ( Image : NQ ) <p> Strasbourg authority underscores this . In Steel and Others v United Kingdom ( 1998 ) , the court recognised that peaceful protest -- even when inconvenient -- is part of the lifeblood of democracy . In cases such as Vajnai v Hungary ( 2008 ) and F @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ warned against criminalising the mere display of symbols or messages absent a clear and present danger . And in Egitim ve Bilim Emek ? ileri Sendikasi v Turkey ( 2012 ) , the court held that wearing clothing to communicate a political message falls squarely within Article 10 protection . The thread through these cases is simple : a democratic state must tolerate robust expression unless there is a pressing social need to penalise it , and the response must be proportionate to that need . <p> Domestic law points the same way while acknowledging Parliament 's terrorism framework . In R v Choudary 2016 EWCA Crim 61 , the Court of Appeal drew a bright line between " inviting support " ( which section 12(1) covers ) and merely sharing an opinion ( which it does not ) . Parliament responded by enacting section 12(1A) , but even there the Court of Appeal in ABJ and BDN v Rex 2024 EWCA Crim 1597 emphasised that the prosecution must prove ( a ) expression supportive of the proscribed organisation and ( b ) recklessness as to encouraging support among the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ proportionality is built into the elements . Meanwhile , the Supreme Court in Pwr v Director of Public Prosecutions 2022 UKSC 2 upheld section 13 as compatible with Article 10 precisely because it targets conduct that reasonably suggests membership/support , not mere political controversy . A T-shirt condemning genocide is not the same thing as a uniform , badge or emblem of a proscribed group . <p> Scots law adds two further safeguards . First , the Lord Advocate and COPFS are public authorities bound by section 6 of the Human Rights Act 1998 and section 57(2) of the Scotland Act 1998 to act compatibly with Convention rights ; prosecutorial discretion must be exercised accordingly . Secondly , the Scottish definition of breach of the peace ( Smith v Donnelly 2001 SCCR 800 ) demands a threshold of conduct severe enough to cause -- or risk causing -- serious disturbance to the community ; criminalising a peaceable T-shirt falls far below that line . <p> None of this is to minimise genuine public-safety concerns . Violence , criminal damage and intimidation are unlawful and should be prosecuted . But conflating @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ beyond the margins and corrodes public confidence in policing . It also risks turning the proscription regime -- already criticised by independent experts and human rights bodies -- into a tool for suppressing controversial viewpoints rather than a necessary response to violent extremism . <p> The Lord Advocate has recently reaffirmed that decisions on these cases will be taken by specialist prosecutors and must be in the public interest . That public interest test is not met where the evidence shows only that a citizen wore a protest T-shirt condemning atrocities and urging action under international law . Indeed , Scotland should lead by example in ensuring that the policing and prosecution of protest are scrupulously compatible with Article 10 , as the Scottish Human Rights Commission has urged in its correspondence with Police Scotland and COPFS . <p> ( Image : Supplied ) <p> Mr Laverty spoke of the " court of public opinion " . That court is not a substitute for the rule of law ; it is a reminder of it . Article 10 guards the space where writers , artists and citizens can speak plainly @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Scotland 's institutions should be proud to defend that space . The Lord Advocate should issue clear guidance to decline or discontinue prosecutions where the evidence does not meet the specific elements of sections 12 or 13 and where criminalisation would be a disproportionate interference with free expression . <p> If we criminalise a message that says , in essence , " stop genocide " , we have lost the plot . The proper response is not a charge sheet but a recommitment to the principle that in a democracy , words -- however uncomfortable -- are met with words , not handcuffs . <h> follow us <p> This website and associated newspapers adhere to the Independent Press Standards Organisation 's Editors ' Code of Practice . On Russia : Trump 's Alaska summit might have ended Putin 's isolation by the West , but the extent of that isolation was exaggerated . If the US can veto accountability for Israel , then Russia can veto accountability for Syria or Ukraine ; China can do the same elsewhere . Atrocities become a currency in the game of global politics , and those who suffer are condemned not by their own actions but by the alliances of those who oppress them . <p> We can no longer pretend that minor reforms will fix this . Only then can we begin to build an international system that does what it was always meant to do : stand for humanity .

The Italians likewise claimed they were " returning " to ancient Roman lands when they conquered Libya , framing their colonisation as merely reclaiming and restoring part of their ancient homeland . <p> Even the German Nazis justified their conquest of Eastern Europe and European Russia as a " return " . They also created Bantustans for the indigenous Namibian population to maintain white supremacy in Namibia during the South African occupation of that country . <p> Like the French , Italians and Germans , Zionists claimed that it was the indigenous Palestinians who were the real colonists of the " ancient homeland " of European Jews , portraying them as the descendants of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ century . <p> But the Arab conquest was not a settler colonial one ; it was missionising and territorially expansionist . <p> Most of the indigenous peoples of Syria and Palestine , who were ruled by the Byzantine Empire and subsequently conquered by the Muslim Arabs , remained the majority after the conquest , including the native Syrian Arabic-speaking Christian Ghassanids . <p> It took some five centuries - in Palestine and Greater Syria , and even longer in Egypt - before most converted to Islam , although Arabisation and adoption of the Arabic language came much earlier , including among the native Christian churches . <p> Very few Arabs moved to the conquered territories , and the few thousand who did mainly settled in the cities . <p> By the time the Crusades - the first true Zionists - conquered Palestine in the 11th century , most of its inhabitants were indigenous Arabic-speaking Christians , with a minority of indigenous Arabic-speaking Muslims . <h> Colonial precedents <p> As late as 1919 , even David Ben-Gurion and Yitzhak Ben-Zvi , the founding fathers of the Jewish settler colony , argued @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in fact , descendants of the ancient Hebrews who had converted first to Christianity and later to Islam . <p> Mistaking Arabness for a racial category rather than a linguistic and cultural identity , the racialised European colonial powers sought to divide the Arabs . Arab nationalism , however , insisted that Arabs were simply those whose mother tongue was Arabic and never claimed that Arabness was a race or an ethnicity . <p> Another common Zionist argument is that Britain was not the " mother country " or " metropole " of the Zionist colonists , since most were not British citizens but came from other European countries . Britain had earlier sponsored the settler colonisation of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ although most of the settlers were Scottish and English . <p> The Dutch colonised southern Africa with Dutch and French Huguenots , though the Dutch predominated .
